content: 1. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) Retinitis in HIV-Infected Adults: Treatment options include intravenous ganciclovir, oral valganciclovir, intravenous foscarnet, intravenous cidofovir, or a combination of an intraocular ganciclovir implant with oral valganciclovir. These regimens are tailored to the severity and progression of the disease. 2. Alternative Treatment for CMV in HIV-Infected Children: For CMV disease or ganciclovir-resistant CMV infections, intravenous foscarnet is recommended. 3. CMV in Transplant Patients: The preferred treatment regimen is oral valganciclovir. 4. CMV Colitis and Esophagitis: Preferred regimen 1: Oral valganciclovir 900 mg once daily. Preferred regimen 2: Oral valganciclovir 900 mg twice daily for 14–21 days, followed by 900 mg once daily for maintenance therapy. Alternative regimen: Intravenous ganciclovir 5 mg/kg twice daily for 14–21 days, with an extended induction period of 3–6 weeks in some cases. Maintenance therapy may not be necessary unless there is a relapse. Responses to treatment are less predictable compared to retinitis. 5. CMV Pneumonia: Preferred regimen: Oral valganciclovir 900 mg twice daily for 14–21 days, followed by 900 mg once daily for maintenance therapy. Alternative regimens include intravenous ganciclovir, intravenous foscarnet, or intravenous cidofovir, depending on the clinical scenario. 6. CMV Encephalitis and Ventriculitis: Treatment typically involves intravenous ganciclovir, with a switch to oral valganciclovir when feasible. 7. Lumbosacral Polyradiculopathy: The treatment approach mirrors that for CMV retinitis, with ganciclovir as the primary agent and a transition to valganciclovir when possible. 8. Mononeuritis Multiplex: Management strategies are similar to those for other CMV-related neurological conditions. 9. Prevention of Opportunistic Infections in Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT): Preemptive therapy involves weekly monitoring of CMV viremia using PCR or antigenemia assays from days 10 to 100 post-transplant. Treatment is initiated if CMV is detected. Prophylaxis for high-risk patients or when rapid CMV detection is unavailable includes intravenous ganciclovir starting from engraftment to day 100. 10. CMV Prophylaxis in Solid Organ Transplantation: Kidney, pancreas, or heart transplant: Oral valganciclovir 900 mg once daily starting by day 10 and continuing to at least day 100. Liver transplant: Intravenous ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir, with caution, starting by day 10 and continuing to at least day 100. Lung transplant: Intravenous ganciclovir for 5–7 days, followed by oral valganciclovir for 3–6 months. 11. Post-Treatment Suppression for CMV Retinitis: For patients with a CD4 count <100/mm³, oral valganciclovir 900 mg once daily is recommended. 12. Severe Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (SARS) from Coronavirus: Supportive therapy is the mainstay of treatment, including careful fluid management, oxygen supplementation, and readiness for intubation and mechanical ventilation if respiratory failure occurs. 13. Enterovirus-Related Aseptic Meningitis: Preferred treatment: Intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG) at a dose of 2 g/kg infused over 24 hours. Alternative treatment: Pleconaril. 14. Parvovirus B19 Infections: Erythema infectiosum: Symptomatic treatment only. Transient aplastic crisis: Supportive care with transfusions and oxygen. Fetal hydrops: Intrauterine blood transfusion. Chronic infection without anemia: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). 15. Ebola Virus Disease: Supportive therapy is the cornerstone of management. 16. Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS): Supportive care in the ICU, including careful fluid management, inotropic and vasopressor support if needed, and oxygen supplementation. Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be administered empirically while awaiting diagnostic confirmation. 17. Hepatitis E Virus: Supportive therapy is usually sufficient as the disease is self-limiting. Hospitalization is required for fulminant hepatitis or symptomatic pregnant women. Prevention includes maintaining water quality standards, proper sanitation, and personal hygiene practices. 18. Rotavirus-Induced Diarrhea: Zinc supplementation reduces the duration and severity of diarrhea. Rehydration with intravenous fluids is essential in cases of severe dehydration or shock. Nutrient-rich foods, including continued breastfeeding, are critical to breaking the cycle of malnutrition and diarrhea. 19. Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) Infections: Preferred regimens include intravenous vancomycin or linezolid, with rifampin added in some cases. Surgical evaluation for abscess drainage is recommended when applicable. 20. Diabetic Foot Osteomyelitis: High-risk MRSA cases are treated with linezolid, daptomycin, or vancomycin. 21. Glycopeptide-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus: Linezolid combined with clindamycin is the preferred regimen, with alternatives including daptomycin or tigecycline. 22. Staphylococcus aureus Prophylaxis: Preventive measures and tailored antibiotic regimens are critical in high-risk scenarios. This detailed explanation provides a comprehensive understanding of the treatment and prevention strategies for various infections, tailored to specific patient populations and clinical scenarios.
